title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This assignment predicts Philadelphia tract poverty rates using the 2019–2023 ACS. I start with four ACS predictors, add spatial features from 2023, and compare models using the same observations and ten-fold cross-validation.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

# Figure size for the report.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 140)
options(timeout = 240, tigris_use_cache = FALSE)




I use the helper supplied in the assignment. Resetting the seed with the same response and the same rows makes the folds comparable across models.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}







Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model = character(), added = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(), notes = character()
)

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 1: Choose your outcome

1A: Pull your outcome and baseline predictors
My outcome is the percentage of people below poverty among people for whom poverty status is determined. The predictors are median household income, bachelor’s-degree attainment, renter share, and median age. None is calculated from the poverty numerator or denominator.


Code
# Load the saved ACS data.
if (file.exists("data/assignment4/acs_2023_raw.rds")) {
  philly_tracts <- readRDS("data/assignment4/acs_2023_raw.rds")
} else {
  philly_tracts <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(
      total_pop = "B01003_001",
      poverty_universe = "B17001_001",
      below_poverty = "B17001_002",
      med_inc = "B19013_001",
      median_age = "B01002_001",
      occupied = "B25003_001", renter = "B25003_003",
      edu_total = "B15003_001",
      ba = "B15003_022", ma = "B15003_023",
      professional = "B15003_024", doctorate = "B15003_025"
    ),
    year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE
  )
}
philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_transform(2272) %>%
  st_make_valid()




Code
philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    y = if_else(poverty_universeE > 0,
                below_povertyE / poverty_universeE * 100, NA_real_),
    y_moe = if_else(poverty_universeE > 0,
      moe_prop(below_povertyE, poverty_universeE,
               below_povertyM, poverty_universeM) * 100, NA_real_),
    y_cv = if_else(y > 0, (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100, NA_real_),
    med_inc_10k = med_incE / 10000,
    pct_ba = if_else(edu_totalE > 0,
      (baE + maE + professionalE + doctorateE) / edu_totalE * 100,
      NA_real_),
    pct_renter = if_else(occupiedE > 0,
                        renterE / occupiedE * 100, NA_real_),
    median_age = median_ageE,
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(y) ~ "Outcome unavailable",
      is.na(y_cv) ~ "CV undefined",
      y_cv < 12 ~ "High",
      y_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Low"
    )
  )


Here, y is measured in percent and y_moe in percentage points. Income is in $10,000 units, age is in years, and the two share predictors are percentages.

  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Poverty rate (%)", y = "Tracts",

Answer: A planning agency could use this outcome to identify places needing further assessment and services. Of 408 tracts, 19 have no defined poverty rate, and 59 of the 389 available estimates have low reliability (15.2%), below the template’s approximate one-third warning threshold. Most estimates have moderate reliability, so the outcome is usable for this exercise but should not be treated as certain.


1C: Decide which tracts to model


Code
tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(
    total_popE > 0,
    !is.na(y),
    !is.na(med_inc_10k), med_inc_10k > 0,
    !is.na(pct_ba), !is.na(pct_renter), !is.na(median_age)
  ) %>%
  arrange(GEOID)

n_initial <- nrow(philly_tracts)
n_model <- nrow(tracts)
excluded_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!GEOID %in% tracts$GEOID) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, total_popE, poverty_universeE,
         y, med_inc_10k, pct_ba, pct_renter, median_age)

knitr::kable(tibble(initial = n_initial, retained = n_model,
                    excluded = n_initial - n_model))

Some excluded tracts have no residents, but others are populated places with missing ACS estimates. One zero-poverty estimate has undefined relative CV; I keep that tract in the models and omit it only from the later CV scatterplot.

Part 2: Baseline model

2A: Look first

Code

  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Adults 25+ with BA or higher (%)", y = "Poverty rate (%)")
ggplot(tracts, aes(pct_renter, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +

  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +

  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Median age (years)", y = "Poverty rate (%)")







Poverty rate versus median income; line is an unadjusted linear fit.







Poverty rate versus bachelor’s-degree attainment among adults 25+.

The income relationship appears curved, making a log-income model worth testing later. These are neighborhood associations, not individual or causal effects.

2C: Where is the baseline wrong?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(resid_m1 = residuals(m1))
baseline_map <- ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m1), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0

  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Baseline model: where it is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = actual above predicted",
       fill = "Residual (pp)")
baseline_map





Baseline fitted residuals: positive/red indicates underprediction and negative/blue indicates overprediction.




Answer: Several central/north-central tracts have large positive residuals, meaning the model underpredicts their poverty rates. The baseline may miss local conditions and differences in location. I therefore test reported residential burglary, shooting victim records, and distance from City Hall. The event layers may capture neighborhood conditions, but their associations do not establish that crime causes poverty.

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal

Carto helper and the two layers
I use residential burglary incidents and shooting victim records dated in 2023. A shooting-victim row represents a victim, not necessarily a separate incident. The SQL filters the dates before download.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0(
    "https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=",
    URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE)
  )
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}




Code
burglary_sql <- paste(
  "SELECT cartodb_id, the_geom, dispatch_date, text_general_code",
  "FROM incidents_part1_part2",
  "WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'",
  "AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"
)
shooting_sql <- paste(
  "SELECT cartodb_id, the_geom, date_ FROM shootings",
  "WHERE date_ >= '2023-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"
)

# Read the saved 2023 event data.
if (file.exists("data/assignment4/residential_burglary_2023.geojson")) {
  burglary_raw <- st_read("data/assignment4/residential_burglary_2023.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
} else {
  burglary_raw <- carto_get(burglary_sql)
}
if (file.exists("data/assignment4/shooting_victims_2023.geojson")) {
  shooting_raw <- st_read("data/assignment4/shooting_victims_2023.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
} else {
  shooting_raw <- carto_get(shooting_sql)
}

burglary <- burglary_raw %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(.)) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))
shooting <- shooting_raw %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(.)) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

layer_audit <- tibble(
  layer = c("Residential burglary incidents", "Shooting victim records"),
  downloaded = c(nrow(burglary_raw), nrow(shooting_raw)),
  missing_location = c(nrow(burglary_raw) - nrow(burglary),
                       nrow(shooting_raw) - nrow(shooting))
)

The records were downloaded retrospectively, so they are historical events rather than a saved snapshot of everything known in 2023.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features

4A: Counting


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))
f2 <- y ~ med_inc_10k + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age + n_burglary
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "Burglary count",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts), notes = "2023 records per tract")




4B: Density


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    n_shooting = lengths(st_intersects(., shooting)),
    shooting_per_1k = n_shooting / total_popE * 1000
  )

f3 <- y ~ med_inc_10k + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age + burglary_per_sqmi
m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "Burglary density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts), notes = "Records per square mile")

f4 <- y ~ med_inc_10k + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age + shooting_per_1k
m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "Shooting victim rate",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts), notes = "Victim records per 1,000 residents")

Counts give zero to tracts without recorded events. Density accounts for area, while the victim rate accounts for population. The population denominator still requires care in small tracts.


4C: Distance to the nearest event


Code
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)
nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, shooting)
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_shooting_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(
    tract_pts, shooting[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE

m5 <- lm(f5, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m5", added = "Nearest shooting distance",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f5, tracts), notes = "Straight-line miles")




4D: Distance to one place


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

f6 <- y ~ med_inc_10k + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age + dist_ch_mi
m6 <- lm(f6, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m6", added = "City Hall distance",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f6, tracts), notes = "Straight-line miles")


The CRS is EPSG 2272, measured in feet. Dividing by 5,280 converts distance to miles. These are distances from an interior representative point, not household-weighted travel times.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features

5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
The income scatterplot suggests a curved relationship. I compare linear income with log income, and test log1p() for burglary density because density can be zero.

Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(med_inc_10k)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Income ($10,000s)", y = "Tracts")
ggplot(tracts, aes(log(med_inc_10k))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "log income", y = "Tracts")
ggplot(tracts, aes(burglary_per_sqmi)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Burglary records per square mile", y = "Tracts")
ggplot(tracts, aes(log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "log(1 + burglary density)", y = "Tracts")







Median income before transformation.







Median income after a natural-log transformation.









Residential burglary density before transformation.







Residential burglary density after log1p, which permits zero counts.







Code
f_log <- y ~ log(med_inc_10k) + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age
m_log <- lm(f_log, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "Log income",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts), notes = "Replace the linear income term")

f_log_density <- y ~ med_inc_10k + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi)
m_log_density <- lm(f_log_density, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m8", added = "Log1p burglary density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log_density, tracts), notes = "Allows zero counts")




5B: Squared terms, for curves


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(dist_ch_mi, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2),
              se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Distance from City Hall (miles)", y = "Poverty rate (%)")





Exploratory quadratic fit between poverty rate and distance from City Hall; this is not an adjusted causal relationship.

  dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2)
m_sq <- lm(f_sq, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m9", added = "Squared City Hall distance",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts),
          notes = "Compare with m6 to isolate the squared term")

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 6: Your final model
I compare a combined model with a simpler version that omits burglary density and nearest-event distance. The decision uses CV RMSE rather than coefficient p-values.


Code
f_combined <- y ~ log(med_inc_10k) + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi) + shooting_per_1k + dist_shooting_mi +
  dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2)
m_combined <- lm(f_combined, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m11", added = "Combined spatial and transformed predictors",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_combined, tracts),
          notes = "Compare with the reduced final model")




Code
f_final <- y ~ log(med_inc_10k) + pct_ba + pct_renter + median_age +
  shooting_per_1k + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2)
m_final <- lm(f_final, data = tracts)
summary(m_final)



Call:

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
I used income, education, renter share, and median age to predict poverty. The baseline RMSE was 8.95 percentage points. Taking the log of income gave the biggest improvement, reducing RMSE to 7.77. City Hall distance was the best individual spatial feature. Burglary counts helped less than expected, probably because large tracts can have more events. The final model had an RMSE of 7.58. Adding more variables did not always make the model better.
The coefficient for median age was -0.288. Holding the other variables the same, a one-year higher median age is associated with 0.288 percentage points lower poverty. For prediction, a tract with a median age five years higher has a predicted poverty rate about 1.44 points lower. This does not mean that age causes poverty to fall.
The final map still shows some underprediction in central/north-central Philadelphia. I would next add information about nearby jobs and how often buses and trains run. Historical employment data and SEPTA schedules could help with this. Distance from City Hall does not tell us whether residents can reach jobs easily.
The last plot does not show that less reliable estimates always have bigger errors. Some error may come from the ACS survey, but the plot cannot tell us how much. There are also 8 negative fitted poverty rates. Since real poverty rates cannot be negative, I would not use this model for policy decisions without more checking.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
1.Among New York counties, we know the least about housing costs in Hamilton County, which has the largest relative margins of error at approximately 11.05%. In addition, Schuyler County, Greene County and Lewis County have high margin of error, at 8.74%, 7.96% and 7.19%, which showes that madian gross rent is not accurate for these countries. 2. This pattern occurs because the ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every resident. Smaller counties get fewer responses. So according to our math knowledge, Its results are less accurate. 3. If we assume that every piece of data is highly accurate, then these very small counties might receive too much or too little funding, leading to either overspending or underspending—which could result in wasted funds or people not receiving sufficient assistance. Rural counties with very small populations, such as Hamilton County, are particularly vulnerable.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
The article by Alfred Lubrano (2018) compares poverty rates in Philadelphia between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates. Because the article does not identify the census tracts that make up each informal neighborhood, I analyze poverty at the census-tract level instead of trying to reproduce its neighborhood values exactly.
I use ACS table B17001, Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age. B17001_001 is the population for whom poverty status is determined, and B17001_002 is the number of people below the poverty level. The poverty rate is therefore B17001_002 / B17001_001. I use ACS 5-year estimates because the article uses them and they are available for census tracts. The periods do not overlap: they cover 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Each figure nevertheless pools five years of survey responses rather than representing a single-year count.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Calculate rates, margins of error, and reliability


Show code
tract_2010 <- philly_2010 |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    tract = NAME,
    universe_2010 = poverty_universeE,
    universe_moe_2010 = poverty_universeM,
    poverty_2010 = below_povertyE,
    poverty_count_moe_2010 = below_povertyM
  )

tract_2017 <- philly_2017 |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    universe_2017 = poverty_universeE,
    universe_moe_2017 = poverty_universeM,
    poverty_2017 = below_povertyE,
    poverty_count_moe_2017 = below_povertyM
  )

tract_poverty <- tract_2010 |>
  inner_join(tract_2017, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(
    rate_2010 = poverty_2010 / universe_2010,
    rate_moe_2010 = moe_prop(
      poverty_2010, universe_2010,
      poverty_count_moe_2010, universe_moe_2010
    ),
    rate_2017 = poverty_2017 / universe_2017,
    rate_moe_2017 = moe_prop(
      poverty_2017, universe_2017,
      poverty_count_moe_2017, universe_moe_2017
    ),
    # ACS MOEs use a 90% confidence level, so divide by 1.645 to obtain SE.
    cv_2010 = (rate_moe_2010 / 1.645) / rate_2010 * 100,
    cv_2017 = (rate_moe_2017 / 1.645) / rate_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2010 = case_when(
      cv_2010 < 12 ~ "● Reliable",
      cv_2010 <= 40 ~ "▲ Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "✖ Unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2017 = case_when(
      cv_2017 < 12 ~ "● Reliable",
      cv_2017 <= 40 ~ "▲ Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "✖ Unreliable"
    ),
    change = rate_2017 - rate_2010,
    change_moe = sqrt(rate_moe_2010^2 + rate_moe_2017^2),
    statistically_detectable = abs(change) > change_moe
  )

# A zero poverty universe means a poverty rate and its CV are undefined.
missing_tracts <- tract_poverty |>
  filter(is.na(rate_2010) | is.na(rate_2017))

analytic_tracts <- tract_poverty |>
  filter(!is.na(rate_2010), !is.na(rate_2017))

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
The article’s statement that Philadelphia had about a 26% poverty rate in the 2013–17 ACS is supported: aggregating the tract estimates gives a rate of about 25.8%, which rounds to 26%. The tract-level evidence also supports the more limited statement that some Philadelphia places experienced measurable changes in estimated poverty rates. Thirty-six tracts had statistically detectable increases, while 27 had detectable decreases.
The broad suggestion that poverty rose robustly throughout Philadelphia is not supported by this tract-level test: 313 of 376 usable tracts have changes that are not distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. The article’s exact claims about Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg cannot be determined from this analysis. Those places are informal neighborhoods, and the article does not publish the tract-to-neighborhood boundaries it used. The Holmesburg claim also requires a separate analysis of poverty among White residents, which is not measured by the all-resident poverty rate used here.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
New five-year Census estimates show that poverty remained widespread in Philadelphia in 2013–17, when about 25.8% of residents with a determined poverty status were below the federal poverty line. At the census-tract level, some places saw statistically detectable changes from 2006–10: 36 tracts had estimated increases and 27 had decreases. In most tracts, however, the estimated change was not distinguishable from sampling error at the 90% confidence level. The data point to uneven change across the city, but they do not by themselves establish the article’s exact claims about informal neighborhoods such as Eastwick or Holmesburg.

We predict single-family sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025. Starting with a structure-only model, we add accessibility, neighborhood, property, and time features, then compare transformations using the same ten validation folds.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Property assessments determine property tax bills, so systematic valuation errors can place an unfair burden on some households. The 2017 Chicago Tribune investigation, “The Tax Divide,” found that lower-value homes in Cook County were often assessed at higher shares of their market value than expensive homes.
In this project, we build a model to predict single-family sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025. We will create spatial features and test whether they improve prediction accuracy and reduce geographic patterns in the errors.


We use separate training and test files.

chicago_test.csv
The remaining houses, without sale prices

We clean and explore the sales, build a structure-only baseline, add spatial and neighborhood features, compare every model in a shared log, map the remaining errors, and examine whether the final predictions are equitable across Chicago neighborhoods.

Load the required packages
Loads the packages used for data wrangling, spatial analysis, modeling, and visualization.

Define reusable helper functions
Creates shared functions for missing-value checks, consistent 10-fold cross-validation, and Chicago Data Portal downloads.


Code
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Impute them or choose another variable.")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Part 2B: Neighborhood and demographic features
A house isn’t worth just its structure and its ride to the L. The neighborhood matters too, so we add Census tract context to every house — the same way for training and test — from the 2019-2023 5-year ACS: median income, poverty, education, owner-occupancy, vacancy, and gross rent. None of these come from sale price.

Download ACS tract data for Cook County
We pull the 2019-2023 5-year ACS estimates for Cook County tracts and put them in the same projection as the sales.


Code
acs_vars <- c(
  B19013_001 = "med_income",                 # median household income ($)
  B17001_001 = "pov_denom", B17001_002 = "pov_count",   # poverty status
  B06009_001 = "edu_denom", B06009_005 = "edu_bach", B06009_006 = "edu_grad", # educ 25+
  B25003_001 = "own_denom", B25003_002 = "own_owner",   # tenure
  B25064_001 = "med_rent",                   # median gross rent ($)
  B25002_001 = "vac_denom", B25002_003 = "vac_vacant"   # vacancy
)
acs_names <- setNames(acs_vars, paste0(names(acs_vars), "E"))

acs_tracts <- get_acs(geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook",
                      variables = names(acs_vars), year = 2023, survey = "acs5",
                      geometry = TRUE, output = "wide", cache_table = TRUE)
acs_tracts <- acs_tracts[c("GEOID", names(acs_names), "geometry")]
names(acs_tracts) <- c("GEOID", unname(acs_vars), "geometry")
acs_tracts <- acs_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    pct_poverty   = pov_count / pov_denom * 100,
    pct_bachelors = (edu_bach + edu_grad) / edu_denom * 100,
    pct_owner_occ = own_owner / own_denom * 100,
    pct_vacant    = vac_vacant / vac_denom * 100
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_income, pct_poverty, pct_bachelors,
         pct_owner_occ, pct_vacant, med_rent, geometry) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(all_sales))

acs_tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% nrow()


Source: 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-year estimates (Census Bureau), pulled with tidycensus. We use the tract as the neighborhood unit — it’s the standard geography for this kind of context, and it’s small enough to show how much Chicago neighborhoods differ.


Map neighborhood income
The map makes one thing obvious: income has a strong spatial gradient that the accessibility features missed entirely.

Adding neighborhood context improved both measures at once. The socioeconomic block on its own (m6) cut CV RMSE by about $23k and Moran’s I by about 0.05; the housing block (m7) helped less. Combining them (m8) did a bit better than either alone, and log-transforming income and rent (m9) landed about the same. The big win was the interaction between building size and log income (m10) — extra square footage is simply worth more where incomes are higher, and an additive model can’t see that. Adding the log-income main effect explicitly (m12) tidied the model up and edged out m10. Our handoff, m12, drops CV RMSE by roughly $50k and Moran’s I by about 0.11 versus Member 1’s model, so the errors no longer cluster the way they did. That’s the neighborhood context Member 3 can build on.

Part 3: Final model

3A: Selected combination
The final model uses the original dollar price as its outcome. It combines log lot size, income and rent; size and age squares; grouped count variables; existing property and time attributes; and coordinate squares and interactions. text:
Part 6: Reflection


Show code
air_beta <- unname(coef(final_fit$fit)["central_air"])


The central-air coefficient is $9,555. Holding the other modeled features fixed, houses with central air are associated with a sale price that is $9,555 higher. For prediction, otherwise identical input records differing only in central air receive predictions that differ by this same dollar amount. This association does not establish the causal effect of installing air conditioning.
The useful changes: logs compress a predictor’s long tail, squares allow a curved relationship, factors allow category differences, and interactions let a relationship vary by place. We keep the outcome in dollars so the model coefficients, predictions, and RMSE remain in dollar units. Better-looking predictor distributions alone are not enough; each choice is assessed using the same validation procedure.
We would not yet deploy the model for assessments. Expensive or unusual transactions still have large errors, residuals remain spatially clustered, and some forecasts are negative. Validation uses random folds rather than future-year or geographic holdouts, and unsold properties may differ from the observed sales. These limitations should accompany the lower CV RMSE.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
We predict single-family sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025. Starting with a structure-only model, we add accessibility, neighborhood, property, and time features, then compare transformations using the same ten validation folds.
The selected model reduces mean ten-fold RMSE from $285,974 for the previous model to $250,171, a 12.5% improvement. The outcome remains the original sale price in dollars throughout. The comparison uses ordinary linear regression with the predictor logs, squared terms, categories, and interactions covered in class.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Part 2: Build and compare models

2A: Keep the outcome in dollars
The Week 7 rule is “Log X, keep Y in dollars.” Every candidate below uses sale_price as its response. We use lm() with predictor logs, squared terms written with I(), factors, and interactions; the model log also tests the pooled neighborhood fixed effects discussed in the lecture.
All candidates use the same 23,099 training sales and the same ten folds as the previous model. We reproduce its CV RMSE of $285,973.56 before comparing changes. Missing property values are filled using each training fold only. RMSE is the average of the ten fold-level RMSEs; MAE, R², and Moran’s I use all out-of-fold predictions.


Show code
xy <- st_coordinates(train_sf)
w <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 5)), style = "W")
base_rhs<-paste('building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +',
 'dist_downtown_mi + dist_cta_mi + mean_3cta_mi + cta_within_half_mile +',
 'log(med_income) + pct_poverty + pct_bachelors + pct_owner_occ + pct_vacant +',
 'log(med_rent) + building_000sf:log(med_income)')
f12<-as.formula(paste('sale_price ~',base_rhs))
set.seed(5080)
reference_fit<-train(f12,data=d,method='lm',trControl=trainControl(method='cv',number=10))
folds<-reference_fit$control$index
stopifnot(abs(reference_fit$results$RMSE-285973.56)<1)

# All candidate responses are the original dollar price.
candidates<-list()
add<-function(id,description,rhs) {
 candidates[[id]]<<-list(id=id,description=description,rhs=rhs)
}
physical<-paste('lotsize_acre + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size +',
 'central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace')

geo_terms<-'lon_c + lat_c + I(lon_c^2) + I(lat_c^2) + lon_c:lat_c'

raw_context<-gsub('log(med_income)','med_income',landlog,fixed=TRUE)

2B: Try changes that have a reason
We first add the existing property, land, and sale-time attributes. We then compare raw versus logged predictors, squares of size and age, and grouped count variables. For location, we test linear coordinates, their squares, and their interaction; area-by-coordinate interactions allow an extra square foot to have different dollar value in different places. Centering longitude at −87.65 and latitude at 41.88 makes the coordinate terms easier to calculate and leaves their model information unchanged.
The alternative tract fixed-effect models use Census tracts as neighborhood categories. Within each training fold, tracts with fewer than 70 sales and unseen validation tracts are pooled into “Other,” following the lecture’s advice to merge sparse categories. No neighboring sale prices, residual lags, or other target-derived predictors are used.


Show code
prepare_fold<-function(tr,va) {
 vars<-c('lotsize_acre','num_half_baths','num_fireplaces','garage_size','warmairfurnace','full_basement')
 for(v in vars){med<-median(tr[[v]],na.rm=TRUE);tr[[v]][is.na(tr[[v]])]<-med;va[[v]][is.na(va[[v]])]<-med}
 # Keep sparse or unseen tract groups pooled; the group rule uses training X only.
 freq<-table(tr$GEOID);common<-names(freq)[freq>=70]
 tr$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(tr$GEOID)&tr$GEOID %in% common,tr$GEOID,'Other')
 va$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(va$GEOID)&va$GEOID %in% common,va$GEOID,'Other')
 add_variables <- function(x) {
  x$lon_c <- x$lon + 87.65
  x$lat_c <- x$lat - 41.88
  x$age_band <- cut(x$building_age,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 5, 20, 50, 80, 110, Inf), right = TRUE,
    labels = c('0-5', '6-20', '21-50', '51-80', '81-110', '111+'))
  x
 }
 tr <- add_variables(tr)
 va <- add_variables(va)
 list(tr=tr,va=va)
}
fit_predict<-function(cand,tr,va) {
 z<-prepare_fold(tr,va)
 f<-as.formula(paste('sale_price ~',cand$rhs))
 fit<-lm(f,data=z$tr)
 pred<-as.numeric(predict(fit,newdata=z$va))
 stopifnot(length(pred)==nrow(va),all(is.finite(pred)))
 list(pred=pred,fit=fit)
}
score<-function(cand,folds,seed=5080) {
 pred<-rep(NA_real_,nrow(d));fr<-numeric(length(folds))
 for(k in seq_along(folds)) {
  ti<-folds[[k]];vi<-setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)),ti)
  pred[vi]<-fit_predict(cand,d[ti,],d[vi,])$pred
  fr[k]<-sqrt(mean((d$sale_price[vi]-pred[vi])^2))
 }
 e<-d$sale_price-pred
 metrics<-data.frame(model=cand$id,description=cand$description,seed=seed,
  cv_rmse=mean(fr),pooled_rmse=sqrt(mean(e^2)),mae=mean(abs(e)),median_ae=median(abs(e)),
  oof_r2=1-sum(e^2)/sum((d$sale_price-mean(d$sale_price))^2),
  moran_i=as.numeric(moran(e,w,n=length(e),S0=Szero(w))$I),negative_oof=sum(pred<0))
 list(metrics=metrics,pred=pred)
}

results <- lapply(candidates, score, folds = folds)
model_log <- bind_rows(lapply(results, `[[`, "metrics")) %>% arrange(cv_rmse)
stopifnot(nrow(model_log) == 24,
  abs(results$m12_reference$metrics$cv_rmse -
